metadata.file_name: Rutkowski et al. - 2024 - The limits of inference reassessing causality in international assessments.pdf
metadata.title: The limits of inference: reassessing causality in international assessments

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This article does not conduct an original student-level analysis of ILSA microdata; instead, it is a conceptual and evaluative review of how quasi-experimental causal claims are (and are not) supported when using ILSA data. Because no analytic dataset is constructed for estimation, there is no sampling frame, no complex survey design, and no application of ILSA student/school weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife). The paper discusses methodological constraints such as country heterogeneity, standardization, and the difficulty of satisfying quasi-experimental assumptions (e.g., equivalence of groups in expectation), rather than providing weighting-based inference. Therefore, weight variables and PV/scaling procedures are not applicable to this paper’s own results, though they are relevant considerations for the cited empirical studies it critiques.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a review/conceptual paper that does not estimate student-level outcomes from ILSA cognitive achievement scores using PV-based models. As a result, plausible values handling is not applicable because there is no PV generation/combination step in the paper’s own analysis. Similarly, missing-data handling is not reported because the paper does not run an empirical estimation pipeline on an ILSA micro-dataset.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No original ILSA microdata sample is analyzed. The paper reviews and discusses methodological issues in quasi-experimental studies that use ILSA data (e.g., PIRLS and PISA in the examples), but it does not define an analytic sample or apply inclusion/exclusion criteria for an estimation dataset.

data.outcome_summary: This paper is not an empirical ML or causal-estimation study using ILSA microdata; it is a methodological critique and framework-oriented review. It argues that the observational, cross-sectional, and standardized nature of ILSA data makes strong causal inference difficult, even when quasi-experimental designs (e.g., difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, fixed effects) are used. The authors juxtapose examples of quasi-experimental studies that can approximate causal reasoning with RCT-like assumptions against ILSA-based applications that face limitations such as non-exogenous treatment exposure across countries, threats to the parallel trends/equivalence-in-expectation condition, and ambiguity in defining treatments and outcomes across heterogeneous contexts. The paper emphasizes that causal claims require stringent, often untestable assumptions and that standardization can mask heterogeneity, limiting policy interpretation. Because no model training, PV handling, weighting, or missing-data strategy is executed in the paper itself, no predictive performance metrics are reported.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse because the manuscript is a conceptual/review article rather than an empirical analysis of ILSA microdata. It does not report an analytic sample size, country-level student counts, PV handling, missing-data procedures, or any ML model training/evaluation. Consequently, fields required for empirical predictive studies (e.g., main_findings rows with metrics) are intentionally empty.
